name: Vector Art
basis: software illustration: k-means flat colours and cleaned borders, as exported SVG (how)

lumenary.blurb: Flat colour shapes with clean edges and no gradients, like an illustration exported as SVG.

facts.bestOn: Portraits and scenes with distinct colour regions

why: A vector illustration is made of shapes rather than pixels, so it has flat colour and crisp, curved edges. A photograph is the opposite, so the job is to find the few colours that describe the picture and then clean up the borders between them. K-means clustering does the first part and a blur-and-snap step does the second.
how: Blur the picture and raise its saturation so that grain does not create islands.
Choose k starting colours, assign every pixel to the nearest, move each colour to the average of its pixels, and repeat.
Give every pixel its cluster’s colour.
Blur the flat image and snap each pixel back to the nearest palette colour, which rounds the staircase corners.
Darken pixels whose neighbour belongs to a different cluster to draw the outline.
history: Ivan Sutherland’s Sketchpad in 1963 showed that a computer could store drawings as geometry. Adobe Illustrator brought vector drawing to designers in 1987, and Scalable Vector Graphics became a web standard around 2001. The k-means method is older still, described by Stuart Lloyd in 1957 and named by James MacQueen in 1967.
uses: Starting points for logos and icons
terms: A method that groups pixels into k clusters by repeatedly averaging.
A group of pixels that are close in colour.
A graphic described by shapes and curves instead of a grid of pixels.
paragraphs: Vector illustrations are flat areas of colour with clean edges, and the way to get that from a photograph is to cut the picture into a small palette. First the picture is blurred (so that grain does not produce islands) and its saturation is raised. Then k-means clustering finds the k colours that best describe it: start with k random colours from the picture, assign every pixel to the nearest one, move each colour to the average of its pixels, and repeat.

Every pixel then takes its cluster’s colour. The edges between clusters are still stair-stepped, so the flat image is blurred and each pixel is snapped back to the nearest palette colour, which rounds the corners. Finally the pixels whose neighbour belongs to a different cluster are darkened to draw the outline. The blurs are written as arithmetic on the pixel arrays rather than as browser filters, so they work in every browser.

equations.tex: c_i\leftarrow\frac{1}{\lvert S_i\rvert}\sum_{p\in S_i}p,\qquad S_i=\{\,p:\ \lVert p-c_i\rVert\le\lVert p-c_j\rVert\ \forall j\,\}
equations.note: One k-means step: assign each pixel to its nearest centre, then move the centre to the mean of its pixels.
Saturation s: each channel moves away from (s > 1) or towards (s < 1) the grey value ℓ.
